title: Election 2026 live updates: Voters head to the polls in a midterm battle for House and Senate control
text:
Election Day 2026 live updates: Midterm polls open as Democrats push to check Trump 
 LIVE COVERAGE Updated 4 minutes ago Election 2026 live updates: Voters head to the polls in a midterm battle for House and Senate control
 Democrats hope to take both chambers from Republicans in an election that is largely a referendum on President Donald Trump’s policies.
 Save Add NBC News to Google Updated November 03, 2026, 11:24 AM EST By NBC News What to know on Election Day 
 CONGRESSIONAL RACES: Control of Congress hangs in the balance as voters head to the polls today in an election in which the economy and the Iran war are key issues for Americans. Recent polling suggests Democrats are in a strong position to retake the House, while the Senate majority could come down to competitive races in traditionally red states.
 KORNACKI: In his latest Data Dive newsletter , Steve looks at the handful of races that could set the tone for the long night ahead.
 TRUMP’S FINAL PUSH: President Donald Trump , whose last two years in office will be influenced by the results, led a series of tele-rallies for Republicans after having campaigned in person dozens of times over the past month. He’s expected to spend the day in Washington and attend an election night watch party at the White House.
 ELECTION RESULTS: Follow along this evening for results, detailed election data , analysis and on-the-ground reporting from correspondents around the country. Steve Kornacki is live at the Big Board starting at 5:30 p.m. ET, and NBC News primetime coverage begins at 6:30 p.m. ET.
 NEW UPDATES 4m ago / 11:24 AM EST Bernie Sanders wants an ‘extremely bold’ agenda if Democrats win Senate 
 Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is in line to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee if Democrats win control of the Senate today.
 “If I have anything to say about it, and I will: The agenda of the Democratic Party is going to be extremely bold. It is going to take on the oligarchs. The super-PACs are not going to run the agenda anymore,” he told reporters recently. “We’re going to do what the American people want.”
 Sanders laid out the priorities he would seek to pursue.
 “At the top of my list will be a fight for Medicare for All, to guarantee health care to every man, woman, and child in this country," he said. "Furthermore, in an economy where 60% of our people are living paycheck to paycheck, we want to raise the minimum wage to a living wage — talking about $20 an hour. When millions of workers want to join unions and are now prohibited by their employers from doing so, I want to pass the PRO Act to make it easier for workers to join unions. And obviously, AI and the huge implications that’s going to happen to American workers and the American people is going to be something that’s high up on the list.”
 13m ago / 11:16 AM EST Vivek Ramaswamy casts his vote in Ohio 
 Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy votes as his wife, Apoorva, looks on today in Upper Arlington.   Jay LaPrete / AP 
 Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur and close ally of Trump, is running against Democrat Amy Acton in the race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.
 19m ago / 11:09 AM EST Despite issues with voting machines in NYC suburbs, no need yet to extend voting hours, official says 
 Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins said in a video message that issues with paper ballots not going through the scanners is being worked on, and there's "not a need at this point in time" to extend voting hours in the New York City suburb. 
 "The Board of Elections has said they want to reassure every voter that their vote matters, and their ballot will be secure and their vote will be counted," the Democrat said, adding the scanner problem "is a county-wide issue." 
 Regardless, "people should understand that their vote will be counted — period, the end," Jenkins said. "So if you are standing in a line or you are planning on going to your polling place, continue to do so and do your vote. Circle in those ballots and then be able to hand those in into the orange bag and be directed by the poll workers, they’ll tell you exactly what you need to do."
 In a separate statement on social media , the state Board of Elections said the county board "is actively working to resolve" the issue "as quickly as possible, and we remain in constant contact with them."
 Show more "Voters should rest assured that there has been no disruption to voting. Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted," the board said. 
 Jenkins said in a written statement, “Once these issues are resolved, I will convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again."
 26m ago / 11:02 AM EST Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control? 
 In 2024, Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed that Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.
 Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term.
 Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s more likely that determining the winners in important races will take time.
 Read the full story here. 
 39m ago / 10:50 AM EST Schumer calls mood on Election Day ‘nauseously optimistic’ after casting his vote 
 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., voted in the midterm election and told reporters, “We don’t want to count our chickens before they hatch.” NBC News’ Julie Tsirkin breaks down what Schumer said after casting his vote.
 Schumer calls mood on Election Day ‘nauseously optimistic’ after casting vote 06:04 
 47m ago / 10:42 AM EST Unknown number of Broward County voters turned away before glitch resolved 
 An unknown number of voters in Broward County, Florida, were turned away this morning after a countywide software glitch left poll workers unable to submit some ballots. 
 At a news conference, Broward County Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott implored anyone who was turned away to return by tonight’s 7 p.m. deadline to cast a ballot. Scott said the issue, which involved a feature designed to help poll workers provide voters with the correct ballots after redistricting, was resolved within 20 minutes.
 Scott said about 45,000 votes had been cast by 10 a.m. Some on social media reported initially being unable to access the county's vote totals online, but the figures eventually appeared. 
 Broward County has more than 1.1 million registered voters. 
 1h ago / 10:28 AM EST Equipment failures in Fulton County, Georgia, may require rescanning some ballots 
 An election official in Georgia says two scanners in Fulton County that experienced equipment failure during early voting last month will require a modified tabulation procedure and the potential rescanning of some of the ballots.
 One scanner that had seen 708 ballots cast on it displayed a paper jam error even after troubleshooting confirmed there was no apparent obstruction, Nadine Williams, an election director in Fulton County, said in a memo. The other scanner had 361 ballots cast on it before a voter accidentally rolled over its power cable with their wheelchair, causing an unexpected shutdown, according to Williams.
 A polling location in Atlanta this morning.   Elijah Nouvelage / Bloomberg via Getty 
 The potential rescanning of the ballots tonight will require the approval of the Fulton County Board of Registration and Elections. Any tabulation would be done publicly and be available to poll watchers when the process begins, Williams added.
 Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger confirmed at a news conference that about 1,000 ballots will need to be rescanned but downplayed the significance of the issue. He added that it will not delay the results.
 "It’s one of those things that can happen, and we have always had procedures in place," he said.
 2h ago / 9:34 AM EST Trump says U.S. will stop $4B in aid to Israel at end of year 
 Trump said this morning that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the U.S. to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel , without providing details.
 The issue of U.S. aid to Israel and Israel’s war in Gaza have been among the most contentious leading up to the midterm elections.
 Oil prices slid in response to Trump’s comments.
 “Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year , and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” the president said in a phone interview with “Fox and Friends,” saying the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.”
 Read the full story here. 
 3h ago / 9:22 AM EST Voting gets underway in the midterm elections 
 Voters are heading to the polls in a critical midterm election that will decide which party controls Congress. NBC News’ Ryan Nobles reports.
 Voting gets underway in the midterm elections 02:50 
 3h ago / 9:09 AM EST DOJ says it has taken 'reasonable efforts' to ensure no sworn law enforcement officers are at polling places 
 The Justice Department's civil rights division this morning assured a federal judge that it's taken “reasonable efforts” to ensure sworn law enforcement officers are not being used as civil rights election monitors. 
 As NBC News has reported , the DOJ is sending a record number of election monitors to polling places in all 50 states for today’s midterm elections. 
 The NAACP and League of United Latin American Citizens had filed suit to block the administration from deploying federal law enforcement agents to the polls, and the DOJ told U.S. District Judge Reggie B. Walton at a hearing yesterday that poll monitors pulled from agencies like the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Prisons and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives would only be administrative or clerical personnel, not “sworn officers” with the authority to effectuate arrests. 
 Show more In the filing today, DOJ attorney Andrew Warden said the DEA had pre-emptively prohibited sworn officers from serving as election monitors, and that the civil rights division “exercised its discretion to subsequently consult with Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the U.S. Marshals Service to ensure no employee from those agencies who were signed up to monitor were sworn law enforcement agents,” and had removed several sworn law enforcement officers who had signed up to volunteer. 
 The civil rights division, Warden added, has concluded that utilizing the Bureau of Prisons employees as monitors "will not create a risk of an arrest at a polling location.”
 At the hearing yesterday, Walton said there would be "hell to pay" if he found out he was misled. 
 3h ago / 9:02 AM EST Will Democrats flip enough seats to gain control of Congress? 
 Voters across the country are set to decide Washington’s balance of power, with Republicans fighting to hold on to the Senate and the House, while Democrats are hoping for a blue wave. NBC News chief data analyst Steve Kornacki joins "TODAY" with a deep dive on the numbers, and "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker gives her analysis on what to expect after polls close this evening.
 Will Democrats Flip Enough Seats to Gain Control of Congress? 05:51 
 3h ago / 8:57 AM EST Issue with paper ballots behind some voting machine difficulties in NYC suburb 
 An issue involving paper ballots is behind at least some of the difficulties reported at polling stations in suburban New York this morning, the Westchester County Board of Elections has said. 
 As voters reported issues of voting machines down at polling stations in the county, located in the Hudson Valley just north of New York City, its board of elections said it was looking the matter. It had earlier put out a statement saying the issue had to do with the "thickness" of the ballots, but retracted that shortly after.
 The board said it was in "constant communication with New York state officials, Westchester County government and poll workers to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible. "It urged voters to go ahead with completing paper ballots, which it said would be placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags that would “remain secured and monitored.”
 The issue could potentially delay the results of the competitive race unfolding between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, whose district includes part of the county, and his Democratic challenger Cait Conley. 
 In a post on X, Conley said there were "technical issues with ballot scanners in Westchester." She added: "But don’t worry: you can still vote and every vote is being counted! Don’t be dissuaded and have your voice heard."
 3h ago / 8:43 AM EST In some Senate battleground states, the cost of gas, groceries and housing are rising faster than the national average 
 From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day.
 In 2024, Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House.
 But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters .
 Read the full story here. 
 3h ago / 8:38 AM EST Where things stand on the alleged 'noncitizen' registered voter lists 
 The administration's belated efforts to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting in some states has ping-ponged across every level of the federal judiciary over the past 24 hours, with the courts largely ordering the government to back off. 
 A polling station in Cleveland, Ohio this morning.   Jon Cherry / Getty 
 The Supreme Court yesterday rejected the administration’s request that California separate out up to 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleges might be submitted by noncitizens. The court acted so quickly that it did not even ask California for its views first, as it normally does of the opposing party in such cases. This decision was ONLY specific to California and that disputed list of 20,000 mail in ballots. 
 At a separate hearing in Northern California, U.S. District Judge U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson asked Justice Department attorney Kenneth Kao about the accuracy of the list of the alleged 20,000 noncitizen voters. 
 At a separate hearing in Northern California, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson asked Justice Department attorney Kenneth Kao about the accuracy of the list of the alleged 20,000 noncitizen voters.
 “Would you agree there is a high error rate?” Thompson asked. “I think that’s a fair statement,” Kao responded. 
 Show more Overnight, a three judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals briefly blocked an order from Thompson that barred the administration from any action nationwide that may threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by the administration to be ineligible to vote. 
 Minutes after the panel issued its ruling, the full 9th Circuit court announced its plans to “rehear” the case, vacating the panel's decision and leaving the lower court order blocking the threats intact. 
 In another decision overnight out of federal court in Washington, D.C., the administration was blocked from “further disclosing, transmitting, or releasing data purporting to constitute lists of individual potential or actual non-citizen voters or registered voters, to any State, county, municipal, or other local official, employee, or officer responsible for administering voter registration, issuing or processing ballots, verifying signatures, or tabulating or certifying votes.”
 In all, that means as of 7 a.m. ET, the Trump administration is blocked from sending letters filled with alleged noncitizen registered voter to states for verification, and from threatening election officials with legal action if they don’t comply with the demands set out in those letters.
 3h ago / 8:28 AM EST Voters report broken voting machines in suburban New York 
 Voters in New York's Westchester County have reported issues with broken voting machines at multiple polling stations this morning, with Attorney General Letitia James' office looking into the matter. 
 Ben Hort, a 58-year-old commercial printer, said he went to his polling station in Greenburgh first thing this morning only to be told the machines weren't working. He said he was given the option of casting a paper ballot or returning to the polling station later.
 "I'll try to go back later. I assume they'll get it straightened out," said Hort, who said he's voting "blue all the way across the board." He said he was concerned, however, that some voters might be deterred by the issue and "aren't gonna vote." 
 Show more Bill Moss, a 67-year-old election inspector at another polling station in Greenburgh, said his location was also facing issues, with all three of its voting machines broken. He said voters were being asked to cast their ballots by hand as "the machines are useless to us right now." 
 James emphasized in a post on X that "Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations," adding: "Your votes will count."
 The problem with the machines could delay the results of the highly competitive race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, whose district includes part of the county, and his Democratic challenger Cait Conley.
 Lawler said in a post on X that officials didn't yet know the cause of the problem, but assured voters that "every ballot will be counted. Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting."
 James said her office was monitoring the issue and was in touch with the state and local boards of elections as they work to resolve it.
 "Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations," she wrote on X. Your votes will count."
 4h ago / 8:06 AM EST Early voters turn out in Pennsylvania 
 Voters wait in line at a polling place in Warrington, Pennsylvania, this morning. 
 Matt Rourke / AP 
 4h ago / 8:00 AM EST Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers commends Rep. Stevens endorsement 
 Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers commended Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens for her surprise endorsement of him and condemned his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed's views on Israel. 
 "His rhetoric is causing angst amongst the Jewish community here in Michigan," Rogers said in an interview on "Fox & Friends." "That’s real. That’s palpable, and you see it when young women have to hide their Star of David to walk across a college campus because they’re getting harassed for being Jewish."
 "That language has consequences, and that’s why we were embracing Jewish Democrats," he added.
 Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed months ago, endorsed Rogers on Sunday after a falling out with the Democratic candidate over her attendance at his final campaign events and after disagreements she had over his views on Israel. 
 Show more In interviews and public debate, El-Sayed has declined to say whether he sees Israel, America's long-standing ally, or Iran as a greater threat to the United States.
 Republicans have stepped up their anti-Muslim rhetoric in the Senate race, prompting accusations of racism and Islamophobia from Democrats.
 In response to the attacks, El-Sayed has stressed his loyalty to the Constitution and said Republicans are diverting attention from voters' concerns about the economy and high cost of living, which has been exacerbated by the Iran war and Trump's trade policies.
 4h ago / 7:44 AM EST DOJ is deploying a record number of monitors on Election Day 
 The Justice Department is sending a record number of election monitors to polling places in all 50 states for today’s midterm elections.
 A voter is checked in to cast their ballot in Atlanta this morning.   Megan Varner / Getty 
 While Democratic and Republican administrations have sent federal workers to observe elections for decades, traditionally their mission has been to help ensure Americans exercise their right to vote. Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, has said monitors would also seek to ensure citizens were voting and their votes weren’t canceled out by someone who “shouldn’t be voting.”
 Read the full story here. 
 4h ago / 7:36 AM EST Supreme Court hears Catholic plea to participate in Colorado preschool program 
 Tackling the latest in a series of cases that pit LGBTQ and religious rights against each other, the Supreme Court today will consider whether Catholic entities should be exempted from the state’s antidiscrimination rules so they can participate in a taxpayer-funded preschool program.
 In the Election Day session, the justices will weigh whether Colorado’s refusal to grant an accommodation violates the religious rights of the Archdiocese of Denver and other plaintiffs under the Constitution’s First Amendment.
 Read the full story here. 
 5h ago / 6:58 AM EST Polls open in Maine, North Carolina and Ohio 
 Polls have opened in Maine, North Carolina and Ohio, three states with Senate races that could determine control of the chamber.
 In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins — the only Senate Republican representing a state Trump lost in 2024 — is seeking a sixth term in a tight race against Democrat Troy Jackson. 
 Voters in Kennebunk, Maine this morning.   Sophie Park / Bloomberg via Getty 
 In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed in 2025 after Vice President JD Vance vacated his seat, is locked in a close race against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
 And in North Carolina, Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper is facing former RNC Chairman Michael Whatley in a seat Democrats are hoping to flip after GOP Sen. Thom Tillis said he would retire. 
 Voters in Oregonia, Ohio, this morning.   Carolyn Kaster / Ap 
 5h ago / 6:45 AM EST Floods and severe weather beset parts of the U.S. on Election Day 
 Flash flooding, heavy rainfall and tornadoes have forced election officials in three different regions across the United States to move polling locations, scrambling Election Day plans in hot-button races.
 At least 18 polling locations were moved across seven Florida counties — including Brevard County, Highlands County, Indian River County, Martin County, Okeechobee County, Palm Beach County and St. Lucie County — after intense rainfall caused flash floods on Monday and into this morning.
 Roads were impassable in several parts of the state’s Atlantic coast after a storm dumped as much as 22 inches of rain in 24 hours in a storm that “ exceeded everyone’s expectations ,” as one forecaster put it.
 Severe storms were moving across Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas overnight today. Forecasters issued a tornado watch that lasted until about 2:45 a.m. local time today .
 Read the full story here. 
 Election Day weather: 'TODAY’s' Al Roker tracks the forecast 01:07 
 5h ago / 6:33 AM EST Haley Stevens defends her endorsement of Mike Rogers, says she is disappointed by her party's response 
 Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who stunned state and national Democrats yesterday by making an eleventh-hour endorsement of GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, published a lengthy post on social media last night calling herself a “proud Democrat” and lashing out at critics in the Democratic Party.
 “My decision to withdraw my endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed and support Mike Rogers has angered many Democrats. I understand why. But it was not impulsive, and it was not made for me by anyone else. It was a decision of conscience,” Stevens wrote on X .
 “Once I concluded that Abdul El-Sayed is not fit to serve in the United States Senate, I had to confront who should,” Stevens wrote. “I chose Mike Rogers, with the hope that he can serve in the tradition of John McCain: a senator willing to put country before party and stand up to his own side when conscience requires it.”
 Stevens had previously called Rogers “ wrong for Michigan ” and said he would be “another rubber stamp” for Trump, adding that “we can’t afford to give MAGA another Senate seat in November.”
 Show more Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel effectively excommunicated Stevens yesterday after her endorsement, saying she was no longer a member of the party and would never be again. House Democrats, meanwhile, are weighing whether to banish her . Stevens wrote tonight that her party’s response had troubled her.
 “I respect Democrats who disagree with my decision and ask for the same respect in return,” Stevens wrote. “We can build a stronger, more welcoming, more courageous Democratic Party. And I plan to help lead that effort.”
 She also denounced people who suggested her change of heart was influenced by her fiancé, Jason Turkish, who had said days before Stevens’ announcement that he planned to vote for Rogers.
 “That is sexism dressed up as political analysis,” Stevens posted. “Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion.”
 Stevens had struggled to defend herself in interviews following the endorsement, one of them in a CNN appearance that fellow Michigan Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell called “one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched.”
 6h ago / 5:55 AM EST NBC News Exit Poll: How it works and how we use the results on election night 
 Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices.
 An exit poll is a survey of voters taken as they leave (or exit) their voting locations. Unlike public opinion polls ahead of elections that predict whether respondents will vote, exit polls capture the views of voters in person on Election Day . Exit polls also reflect the views of people who voted early or by mail — we take steps to reach those voters by phone and by mail, as well as online.
 Here’s how exit polls work, where they are conducted and how NBC News will be using the results on election night and in the days after.
 Read the full story here. 
 6h ago / 5:55 AM EST How to watch election night: Key races, poll closing times, bellwether campaigns and more 
 Election night promises to reveal where the country is headed and how the balance of power in Washington will shift — but key results may not trickle out until into the wee hours of tomorrow morning.
 The midterms are largely a referendum on Trump, whose approval rating has languished as voters express frustration over his handling of the economy and the Iran war. Though Democrats are riding a wave of momentum and have held a consistent and significant national polling lead for most of the cycle, whether that is enough to retake control of Congress is not a foregone conclusion.
 In the House, a Democratic majority would require the party to win virtually every seat Trump won by 5 percentage points or less in 2024 — an outcome in line with the findings in recent polls. Control of the Senate is less certain, since Democrats must win at least two states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
 Here’s a guide for how to read the results as they roll in and how to untangle the top dynamics shaping the election in different parts of the country.
 Read the full story here. 
 6h ago / 5:55 AM EST DOJ will deploy a record number of monitors on Election Day 
 The Justice Department plans to send a record number of election monitors to polling places in all 50 states for today's midterm elections.
 While Democratic and Republican administrations have sent federal workers to observe elections for decades, traditionally their mission has been to help ensure Americans exercise their right to vote. Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, has said monitors would also seek to ensure that citizens were voting and that their votes weren’t canceled out by someone who “shouldn’t be voting.”
 Though election monitors are just observers, there has been occasional pushback from states; in 2024, Republican-led Texas, Florida and Missouri sought to block the Democratic Biden administration from sending monitors, arguing that their state laws did not permit federal officials to be at polling places.
 This year, there will be roughly 1,000 monitors nationwide, according to the Justice Department. By comparison, 289 were deployed for the 2022 midterms and 714 for the 2024 presidential election.
